mainTopic: A series of debates in which חכמים answer an emperor, priests and heretics who mock God, creation, the שכינה and ישראל.
overview: This amud opens by finishing a list of three פסוקים connected to רבי מאיר's parables. Then comes a long series of debates in which a Roman emperor, Persian priests and heretics mock God or the Torah, and חכמים answer them, often with a clever demonstration. The emperor's daughter defends the creation of חוה, and רבן גמליאל shows the emperor that he cannot know what is in heaven, cannot count the stars, and cannot explain away one Creator. אמימר and רבי תנחום answer other challenges, and a miracle saves רבי תנחום from wild animals. רבן גמליאל uses the sun to explain how the שכינה rests on every group of ten. רבי אבהו explains יחזקאל's strange commands through the sin of not keeping שמיטה, and shows that God 'immerses' in fire. The amud ends as רבי אבינא begins answering a heretic who denies that ישראל is special, and the פסוק he quotes continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The three verses behind the parables
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes a list of three פסוקים that go with the parables mentioned just before.
steps.simpleTranslation: These are the verses: 'The fathers ate sour grapes and the children's teeth are set on edge'; 'Just balances, just weights'; 'The righteous is saved from trouble, and the wicked comes in his place.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a list that began on the previous page. It names the three פסוקים that the remembered parables were built around.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just before this, the גמרא said רבי מאיר knew many fox parables but only three were remembered. Here it lists the three verses those parables explained. All three are about reward, punishment and fairness: who pays for whose actions.

keyTerms.meaning: Will be set on edge (teeth feeling dull and sore)

phrases.english: "The fathers eat sour grapes
phrases.notes: יחזקאל 18:2

phrases.english: and the children's teeth are set on edge";
"Just balances, just weights";
phrases.notes: ויקרא 19:36

phrases.english: "The righteous is delivered out of trouble,
phrases.notes: משלי 11:8

phrases.english: and the wicked comes in his stead."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָבוֹת יֹאכְלוּ בֹסֶר וְשִׁנֵּי בָנִים תִּקְהֶינָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a list begun before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The three remembered parables explained these three פסוקים.

steps.title: The emperor calls God a thief
steps.stepSummary: The emperor tells רבן גמליאל that God is a thief, because He took אדם הראשון's rib while he slept.
steps.simpleTranslation: The emperor said to רבן גמליאל: Your God is a thief, because it says, 'God made a deep sleep fall on the man and he slept' (and then took his rib).
steps.whatsHappening: A new story begins. The emperor attacks the Torah's story of creating חוה, claiming that it shows God stealing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The emperor's point is that taking something from a sleeping person, without asking, is what a thief does. The פסוק he quotes goes on to say God took one of אדם's ribs, so he reads the sleep as a way of sneaking it away.

keyTerms.meaning: A thief, someone who steals secretly

phrases.english: The emperor said to Rabban Gamliel:
Your God is a thief,
as it is written: "And the Lord God caused a deep sleep to fall
phrases.notes: בראשית 2:21. The rest of that פסוק says God then took one of אדם's ribs.

phrases.english: upon the man, and he slept."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new story, not connected to the list before it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The way God created חוה in בראשית
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Taking a rib from a sleeping person without his knowing looks like stealing.

steps.title: The daughter tells of 'robbers' who left gold
steps.stepSummary: The emperor's daughter offers to answer. She describes robbers who took a silver jug and left a gold one, and her father says he wishes they came every day.
steps.simpleTranslation: His daughter said to רבן גמליאל: Leave him, I'll answer him. She said to her father: Give me an officer. He asked: Why? She said: Robbers came last night, took a silver jug and left a gold one. He said: I wish they would come every day!
steps.whatsHappening: The daughter is setting a trap for her father. She tells a story that gets him to admit that this kind of 'stealing' is actually good, which prepares her answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: She pretends to want revenge on the robbers, so her father will judge the case honestly. Since they left something worth more than what they took, he says such 'robbers' are welcome. Without realizing it, he has now agreed to the idea she will use against him.

phrases.english: His daughter said to him:
phrases.notes: This is the emperor's daughter, speaking to רבן גמליאל.

phrases.english: Leave him, for I will answer him.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרָה לֵיהּ: תְּנוּ לִי דּוּכּוֹס אֶחָד.
phrases.english: She said to him: Give me one commander.
phrases.notes: Now she is turning to her father, asking for an officer as if to go after someone.

phrases.english: He said to her: Why do you need him?
Bandits came upon us tonight
and took from us a silver jug
and left us a golden jug.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהּ: וּלְוַואי שֶׁיָּבֹאוּ עָלֵינוּ בְּכׇל יוֹם.
phrases.english: He said to her: If only they would come upon us every day!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Prepares the answer to the emperor's charge in step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Taking something and leaving something better in its place is a welcome gift, not a harm.

steps.title: Adam got something better than a rib
steps.stepSummary: The daughter applies her story: God took one rib from אדם and gave him a wife to help him, which was good for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Wasn't it good for אדם הראשון that one rib was taken from him and he was given a helper to serve him?
steps.whatsHappening: The daughter answers the 'thief' charge. She points out that אדם gained far more than he lost.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the robbers who left gold for silver, God took a small rib and gave אדם a whole partner. A thief makes you lose; here אדם came out ahead, so the charge of stealing falls apart.

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא יָפֶה הָיָה לוֹ לְאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן,
phrases.english: And was it not good for Adam the first man,
that they took from him one rib
and gave him a maidservant to serve him?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא יָפֶה הָיָה לוֹ לְאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the robber story of step 3 to the emperor's charge in step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Analogy: an exchange for something better is not theft.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Taking the rib was a loss to אדם, like stealing.
steps.terutzMaskana: אדם gained a partner worth much more than a rib, so it was a gift.

steps.title: Then why not take it openly?
steps.stepSummary: The emperor says his real point was different: if it was good for אדם, why did God take it while he slept instead of openly?
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to her: That's what I meant. Let Him take it openly!
steps.whatsHappening: The emperor sharpens his question. He accepts that אדם gained, but asks why it was done in secret.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new target is not the taking itself but the hiding. Doing something while a person sleeps still looks like a thief's way, even if the result is good.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what I was saying (what I really meant)

phrases.english: He said to her: This is what I was saying:
But let Him take it openly!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Refines the original charge after step 4 answered it.
steps.kashyaTarget: Why the rib was taken while אדם slept
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the exchange was good, there was no need to hide it; secrecy suggests theft.

steps.title: The raw meat demonstration
steps.stepSummary: The daughter has raw meat brought, roasts it in front of her father, and offers it to him. He refuses because watching it be prepared made it disgusting to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: She said: Bring me a piece of raw meat. They brought it. She put it under the coals, took it out, and said: Eat. He said: It disgusts me.
steps.whatsHappening: The daughter sets up a live demonstration. It prepares her final answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Roasted meat is normally fine to eat. But since the emperor saw it raw and watched it being made, he no longer wanted it. Seeing how something is made can ruin your desire for it.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרָה לֵיהּ: אַיְיתוֹ לִי אוּמְצָא דְּבִישְׂרָא.
phrases.english: She said to him: Bring me a piece of raw meat.
They brought it to her.
She placed it under the embers, and took it out.
She said to him: Eat (from this).
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the words in round brackets.

phrases.english: He said to her: It is repulsive to me.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Prepares the answer to the question of step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Watching something being prepared can make it repulsive, even when the finished product is good.

steps.title: Why אדם had to be asleep
steps.stepSummary: The daughter explains: if אדם had watched חוה being taken from him, she would have been repulsive to him too.
steps.simpleTranslation: She said: With אדם הראשון too, if she had been taken openly, she would have been repulsive to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The daughter answers the emperor's second question. The sleep was not to hide a theft but to protect אדם's feelings toward his wife.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just as the emperor lost his appetite after watching the meat roast, אדם would have been put off by his wife had he watched her formed from his body. So God did it while he slept, for אדם's own good.
steps.whatToRemember: The emperor's two charges each get an answer: the taking was a gain for אדם (silver for gold), and the secrecy was for אדם's benefit (the raw meat).

phrases.english: She said to him: And Adam the first man as well,
had she been taken openly,
she would have been repulsive to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן נָמֵי, אִי הֲוָת שְׁקִילָה בְּהֶדְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the meat demonstration of step 6 to the question of step 5.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The sleep was a way to take the rib in secret, like a thief.
steps.terutzMaskana: The sleep protected אדם from finding his wife repulsive.

steps.title: The emperor claims to know God
steps.stepSummary: A new story: the emperor boasts to רבן גמליאל that he knows what God does and where He sits.
steps.simpleTranslation: The emperor said to רבן גמליאל: I know what your God does and where He sits.
steps.whatsHappening: A second story begins with a bold claim from the emperor. The next steps will show that the claim is empty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The emperor talks about God as if He were a ruler whose actions and location can be known. רבן גמליאל will answer this not with an argument but with a test.

phrases.english: The emperor said to Rabban Gamliel:
I know your God,
what He does and where He sits.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָדַעְנָא אֱלָהַיְיכוּ מַאי קָא עָבֵיד וְהֵיכָן יָתֵיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new exchange between the same two people.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The emperor claims he can know God's actions and place.

steps.title: The emperor cannot find his own son
steps.stepSummary: The emperor groans; רבן גמליאל asks why. He misses his son overseas. רבן גמליאל asks to be shown the son, and the emperor admits he doesn't know where he is.
steps.simpleTranslation: The emperor was sighing and groaning. רבן גמליאל asked: What is this? He said: I have a son in the cities overseas and I miss him. רבן גמליאל said: I want you to show him to me. The emperor said: Do I know where he is?
steps.whatsHappening: רבן גמליאל leads the emperor, step by step, to admit he doesn't know where his own son is. This sets up the punchline in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן גמליאל's request to see the son seems strange, but it is a trap. It forces the emperor to say out loud that he cannot locate even a person he loves who lives on earth.

phrases.english: He was moaning and groaning.
He said to him: What is this?
phrases.notes: רבן גמליאל is asking the emperor why he is groaning.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: בֵּן אֶחָד יֵשׁ לִי בִּכְרַכֵּי הַיָּם
phrases.english: He said to him: I have one son in the cities overseas
and I miss him.
I want you to show him to me.
phrases.notes: The text doesn't say so, but this is רבן גמליאל speaking now.

phrases.english: He said: Do I know where he is?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Prepares the answer to the emperor's claim in step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Where the emperor's son is, so that he can be shown.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The emperor admits he does not know.

steps.title: If not on earth, surely not in heaven
steps.stepSummary: רבן גמליאל concludes: you don't know what is on earth, yet you claim to know what is in heaven?
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: What is on earth you don't know, and what is in heaven you do know?
steps.whatsHappening: רבן גמליאל knocks down the emperor's boast. The emperor's own admission proves he cannot know God.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a simple 'all the more so' argument. If a person can't locate his own son in this world, he certainly can't claim to know where God sits and what He does.
steps.whatToRemember: The emperor's claim to know God is rejected by his own admission: someone who can't find his son on earth cannot claim to know what is in heaven.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: דְּאִיכָּא בְּאַרְעָא לָא יָדְעַתְּ,
phrases.english: He said to him: What is on earth you do not know,
and what is in heaven you do know?

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאִיכָּא בְּאַרְעָא לָא יָדְעַתְּ, דְּאִיכָּא בִּשְׁמַיָּא יָדְעַתְּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the admission from step 9 to reject the claim of step 8.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The emperor's whole claim to know God's actions and place.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: He can't even know hidden things on earth, so he certainly can't know what is in heaven.

steps.title: The emperor mocks the verse about counting stars
steps.stepSummary: The emperor quotes a פסוק praising God for counting the stars and claims he can do it too.
steps.simpleTranslation: The emperor said to רבן גמליאל: It says God 'counts the number of the stars.' What's so great about that? I can count the stars too!
steps.whatsHappening: A new exchange begins. The emperor attacks a פסוק by saying the praise it gives God is nothing special.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The emperor is not asking for information. He is trying to make God's greatness look small, because any human can count stars. This sets up רבן גמליאל's answer.

keyTerms.meaning: What is His greatness? What is so special?

phrases.english: The emperor said to Rabban Gamliel:
It is written: "He counts the number of the stars";
phrases.notes: תהלים 147:4

phrases.english: What is His greatness?
I can count the stars!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי רְבוּתֵיהּ? אֲנָא מָצֵינָא לְמִימְנֵי כּוֹכְבֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story with the same characters as steps 8-10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The praise of God in the פסוק 'מונה מספר לכוכבים'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a human can count the stars, counting them is no sign of divine greatness.

steps.title: The spinning quinces in a sieve
steps.stepSummary: רבן גמליאל spins quinces in a sieve. The emperor cannot count them, and רבן גמליאל explains that the sky spins the same way.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן גמליאל brought quinces, put them in a sieve and spun them around. He said: Count them. The emperor said: Make them stand still! He answered: The sky also spins like this.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן גמליאל answers the emperor with a hands-on demonstration instead of an argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Things that keep moving cannot be counted by a person. The stars move with the turning sky, so only God can truly count them. The praise in the פסוק stands.

phrases.english: He brought quinces,
phrases.notes: "He" here is רבן גמליאל.

phrases.english: put them in a sieve,
and spun them around.
He said to him: Count them.
He said to him: Make them stand still!

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: רָקִיעַ נָמֵי הָכִי הָדְרָא.
phrases.english: He said to him: The sky also spins like this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the emperor's challenge in step 11.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Counting stars is easy, so God's counting is nothing special.
steps.terutzMaskana: The stars keep moving, so no human can count them. Only God can.

steps.title: Another version: the emperor claims he counted the stars
steps.stepSummary: A second version of the story: the emperor boasts that he has already counted the stars.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say this is what the emperor said: I have counted the stars.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different version of the story. This line sets up רבן גמליאל's reply in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, the emperor does not just say he could count the stars. He says he already did. That changes how רבן גמליאל answers him.

keyTerms.meaning: Some say; another version of the story

phrases.english: Some say that this is what he said to him:
I have counted the stars.
phrases.notes: Literally "the stars are counted by me". The emperor is boasting.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Retells steps 11-12 in a different way.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The emperor claims he has counted the stars.

steps.title: How many teeth do you have?
steps.stepSummary: רבן גמליאל asks the emperor how many teeth he has. The emperor has to count them with his hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Tell me, how many teeth and incisors do you have? The emperor put his hand in his mouth and started counting them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן גמליאל asks a simple question to set a trap. The emperor's answer sets up the punchline in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The emperor does not know how many teeth he has without checking. This shows how little he really knows, even about his own body.

phrases.english: He said to him: Tell me,
your teeth and incisors, how many are they?
He put his hand into his mouth
and was counting them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵימָא לִי כַּכָּיךְ וְשִׁינָּיךְ כַּמָּה הָוֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבן גמליאל responds to the boast in step 13.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The number of the emperor's own teeth
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The emperor does not know and has to count them by hand.

steps.title: You don't know your mouth but you know the sky?
steps.stepSummary: רבן גמליאל points out that the emperor does not know what is in his own mouth, so he cannot claim to know what is in the sky.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: You don't know what is in your mouth, and you know what is in the sky?
steps.whatsHappening: רבן גמליאל knocks down the emperor's boast with the result of his own question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This works like a קל וחומר: if something close and simple, like your teeth, is unknown to you, then something far and huge, like the stars, is surely unknown to you. It matches the pattern from step 10.
steps.whatToRemember: In both versions, רבן גמליאל shows that counting the stars is beyond any human, so the praise in the פסוק is real.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: דְּאִיכָּא בְּפוּמָּיךְ לָא יָדְעַתְּ,
phrases.english: He said to him: What is in your mouth you do not know,
yet what is in the sky you know?

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאִיכָּא בְּפוּמָּיךְ לָא יָדְעַתְּ, דְּאִיכָּא בִּרְקִיעָא יָדְעַתְּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the counting in step 14.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The emperor's claim that he counted the stars
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: He cannot even count his own teeth without checking, so he cannot know the stars.

steps.title: The emperor claims mountains and wind had different creators
steps.stepSummary: The emperor argues from a פסוק in עמוס that one power formed the mountains and a different one created the wind.
steps.simpleTranslation: The emperor said to רבן גמליאל: The one who made the mountains did not make the wind, as it says, 'For behold, He forms mountains and creates wind.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new challenge begins. The emperor uses a פסוק to argue that there was more than one creator.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His proof is the two different verbs in the פסוק: 'forms' (יוצר) for mountains and 'creates' (בורא) for wind. He reads each verb as pointing to a different god.

phrases.english: The emperor said to Rabban Gamliel:

phrases.aramaic: מִי שֶׁבָּרָא הָרִים לֹא בָּרָא רוּחַ,
phrases.english: He who created mountains did not create wind,
as it is stated: "For behold, He forms mountains
and creates wind."
phrases.notes: עמוס 4:13

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי שֶׁבָּרָא הָרִים לֹא בָּרָא רוּחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new exchange on a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Different verbs in the פסוק mean different creators.

steps.title: Then man would also have two creators
steps.stepSummary: רבן גמליאל points out that the תורה uses both 'created' and 'formed' about אדם, so by the emperor's logic one person would have two creators.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, about אדם it says 'And He created' and also 'And He formed.' Would you say that the one who made this part did not make that part?
steps.whatsHappening: רבן גמליאל pushes back by applying the emperor's own rule to another פסוק, to show it leads somewhere silly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If two verbs mean two gods, then אדם, a single person, would have two makers. That result sounds absurd, so the emperor's reading looks wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: If so, then... (introduces a silly result of someone's logic)

phrases.english: If that is so,
phrases.notes: Now רבן גמליאל is the one speaking.

phrases.english: regarding man, where it is written "And He created" and "And He formed,"
phrases.notes: בראשית 1:27 and בראשית 2:7

phrases.aramaic: הָכִי נָמֵי מִי שֶׁבָּרָא זֶה לֹא בָּרָא זֶה?
phrases.english: so too, would He who created this not have created that?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reading method used in step 16.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The rule that two verbs mean two creators
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It would mean that one human being had two creators.

steps.title: Even the small face would need several creators
steps.stepSummary: רבן גמליאל narrows it further: a face is just one handbreadth wide, yet a פסוק uses different verbs for the ear and the eye. Did different gods make them?
steps.simpleTranslation: A person's face is one handbreadth by one handbreadth, and it has two kinds of openings in it. Would the one who made this not have made that? As it says: 'He who planted the ear, shall He not hear? He who formed the eye, shall He not see?'
steps.whatsHappening: רבן גמליאל makes the silly result even sharper by pointing to a tiny area of the body, the face.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The emperor might accept that different body parts had different makers. So רבן גמליאל shows that even inside one small face, the ears and the eyes would need separate gods. That sounds even more far-fetched.

keyTerms.meaning: A handbreadth (a small measure, about a hand's width)

phrases.aramaic: טֶפַח עַל טֶפַח יֵשׁ בּוֹ בָּאָדָם,
phrases.english: A person has a handbreadth by a handbreadth,
phrases.notes: He means the face, a small area of the body.

phrases.english: and it has two kinds of openings in it.

phrases.aramaic: מִי שֶׁבָּרָא זֶה לֹא בָּרָא זֶה?
phrases.english: Would He who created this not have created that?
As it is stated: "He who planted the ear, shall He not hear?
If He formed the eye, shall He not see?"
phrases.notes: תהלים 94:9

steps.triggerLanguage: טֶפַח עַל טֶפַח יֵשׁ בּוֹ בָּאָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sharpens the challenge from step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: The emperor's theory of many creators
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Even one small face would need separate creators for its ears and eyes.

steps.title: The emperor accepts it
steps.stepSummary: The emperor says yes: even the eye and the ear had different creators.
steps.simpleTranslation: The emperor said to him: Yes.
steps.whatsHappening: The emperor does not back down. He accepts even the strange result. This sets up רבן גמליאל's final blow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By saying yes, the emperor stays loyal to his theory. But now he is committed to many gods working on one person, and that opens the door to the next question.

phrases.english: He said to him: Yes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 18.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes, different gods made different parts of the face.

steps.title: Do all the creators agree when a person dies?
steps.stepSummary: רבן גמליאל asks: if many gods each made a part of a person, how do they all agree to let that person die at the same moment?
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: And at the time of death, are all of them satisfied together?
steps.whatsHappening: רבן גמליאל gives the final answer that shows the emperor's theory cannot work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person dies all at once, as one whole. If each part belonged to a different god, they would all have to agree at the exact same moment. That one moment of death shows there is one Creator.
steps.whatToRemember: רבן גמליאל defeats the 'many creators' idea step by step: two verbs for אדם, then two verbs inside one face, and finally the single moment of death, which shows one Creator.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: וּבִשְׁעַת מִיתָה כּוּלָּן נִתְפַּיְּיסוּ?
phrases.english: He said to him: And at the time of death, are all of them satisfied together?
phrases.notes: He means: do all those gods agree at the same moment that this person should die?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the emperor's 'yes' in step 19 against him.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole theory of many creators
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A person dies all at once, which would require all the separate creators to agree at the same moment. That points to one Creator.

steps.title: A Persian priest splits the body between two gods
steps.stepSummary: A Persian priest tells אמימר that the top half of a person belongs to the good god הורמיז and the bottom half to the bad god אהורמיז.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain Persian priest said to אמימר: From your middle and up belongs to הורמיז; from your middle and down belongs to אהורמיז.
steps.whatsHappening: A new story begins. A Persian priest offers his own version of the 'two creators' idea, splitting the human body in half.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same type of claim we just saw with קיסר and רבן גמליאל: different parts of a person come from different powers. Here the split is upper half versus lower half, with the important organs credited to the good god.

keyTerms.meaning: The Persian god they called the god of good
The Persian god they called the god of bad

phrases.english: A certain Persian priest said to Ameimar:
From your middle and up belongs to Hurmiz,
from your middle and down belongs to Ahurmiz.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story with the same theme as steps 16-20: a claim that the human body has more than one creator.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The priest claims the upper body belongs to a good god and the lower body to a bad god.

steps.title: אמימר: then why does one god let the other pass water through his land?
steps.stepSummary: אמימר answers that if so, the bad god should never allow the good god's water to pass through his territory.
steps.simpleTranslation: אמימר said to him: If so, how does אהורמיז let הורמיז pass water through his land?
steps.whatsHappening: אמימר knocks down the priest's claim with a simple bodily fact.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person drinks through the mouth, which is in the upper half, and the water leaves through the lower half. If two rival gods owned the two halves, they would have to cooperate all day long. That shows the body works as one system made by one Creator.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (if your claim were true)

phrases.english: He said to him: If so,
how does Ahurmiz allow Hurmiz
to pass water through his land?
phrases.notes: Water you drink goes in up top (הורמיז's half) and comes out below (אהורמיז's half).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the priest's claim from step 21.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole idea that two rival gods own the two halves of the body.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The two halves constantly depend on each other, which makes no sense if they belong to rival gods.

steps.title: The emperor invites רבי תנחום to make everyone one people
steps.stepSummary: קיסר proposes to רבי תנחום that Jews and Romans join together as one nation.
steps.simpleTranslation: קיסר said to רבי תנחום: Come, let us all become one people.
steps.whatsHappening: A new story begins. קיסר makes an offer that sounds friendly but really means the Jews should give up being different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The emperor's suggestion is a test: becoming 'one people' would mean the Jews joining Roman ways. This sets up רבי תנחום's clever reply.

phrases.english: The emperor said to Rabbi Tanchum:
Come, let us all be one people.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new, separate story about a debate with the emperor.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The emperor proposes that Jews and Romans merge into one nation.

steps.title: רבי תנחום: fine, but you become circumcised like us
steps.stepSummary: רבי תנחום agrees in principle but turns the offer around: Jews cannot undo מילה, so the Romans should circumcise and become like the Jews.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Very well. But we, who are circumcised, cannot become like you. You circumcise yourselves and become like us!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי תנחום accepts the idea of 'one people' but flips who has to change.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מילה cannot be undone, so the only way to become one people is for the Romans to join the Jews. This answer cleverly traps the emperor with his own proposal.

phrases.english: He said: Very well,
we, who are circumcised,
cannot become like you.
You circumcise yourselves and become like us!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the emperor's proposal in step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Agreement in principle, but the Romans must be the ones to change, since מילה cannot be reversed.

steps.title: The emperor admits he lost and throws רבי תנחום to the beasts
steps.stepSummary: קיסר admits רבי תנחום argued well, but rules that anyone who beats the king in debate is thrown to wild animals. The animals do not eat him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: You argued well, but whoever beats the king is thrown into the wild-animal pit. They threw him in, and the animals did not eat him.
steps.whatsHappening: The emperor cannot answer the argument, so he punishes רבי תנחום instead. A miracle saves him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The emperor openly admits the logic is right but uses power instead of reasoning. The animals leaving רבי תנחום alone shows that God protected him.

keyTerms.meaning: You are speaking well (your argument is good)
Who beats the king (in an argument)

phrases.english: He said to him: As far as the argument, you speak well,
but anyone who bests the king
is thrown into the animal enclosure.
They threw him into the enclosure, and they did not eat him.
phrases.notes: 'They' who didn't eat him are the wild animals in the pit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The emperor reacts to losing the debate in step 24.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The emperor concedes the argument but punishes the winner; the animals miraculously spare him.

steps.title: A heretic says the animals weren't hungry, and is eaten himself
steps.stepSummary: A heretic claims the miracle was only because the animals were not hungry. They throw the heretic in, and the animals eat him.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain heretic said to him: They didn't eat him only because they aren't hungry. They threw the heretic himself in, and the animals ate him.
steps.whatsHappening: A heretic tries to explain away the miracle, and his explanation is disproved on the spot.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The heretic says nature, not God, saved רבי תנחום. When he is thrown in and eaten, it proves the animals were hungry and the first rescue was truly a miracle.

phrases.english: A certain heretic said to him:
phrases.notes: He's talking to the emperor.

phrases.english: This, that they did not eat him,
is because they are not hungry.
They threw him himself in, and they ate him.

steps.whatToRemember: Losing an argument, the emperor turned to force, but God protected רבי תנחום, and the heretic's attempt to deny the miracle was proven false.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the miracle of step 25, and the challenge is disproved.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The claim that the animals simply were not hungry.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The animals immediately ate the heretic, so they were hungry after all.

steps.title: The emperor mocks: how many Divine Presences are there?
steps.stepSummary: קיסר challenges רבן גמליאל: if the שכינה rests on every group of ten Jews, there must be many שכינות.
steps.simpleTranslation: קיסר said to רבן גמליאל: You say that the שכינה rests on every group of ten. How many שכינות are there?
steps.whatsHappening: A new story begins with a mocking question from the emperor about how God can be in many places at once.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The emperor assumes something can only be in one place at a time. If the שכינה is with every minyan, he argues, there must be many of them, which goes against the idea of one God.

phrases.english: The emperor said to Rabban Gamliel:
You say that on every group of ten
the Divine Presence rests,
how many Divine Presences are there?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ קֵיסָר לְרַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל: אָמְרִיתוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story with a different challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: The teaching that the שכינה rests on every group of ten.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the שכינה is in many places at once, there must be many שכינות, not one God.

steps.title: רבן גמליאל scolds the servant for letting the sun in
steps.stepSummary: רבן גמליאל calls over the emperor's servant, smacks him on the neck, and asks why he let the sun into the emperor's house.
steps.simpleTranslation: He called the emperor's servant and hit him on the neck. He said to him: Why did the sun come into the emperor's house?
steps.whatsHappening: רבן גמליאל doesn't answer directly. He sets up a demonstration to lead the emperor to the answer himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Blaming the servant for the sun entering is deliberately absurd. It forces the emperor to say out loud that one thing can be everywhere at once, which is the point רבן גמליאל needs.

phrases.english: He called his servant,
phrases.notes: He means the emperor's servant, and it's רבן גמליאל doing the calling.

phrases.english: and struck him on the neck.
He said to him: Why did the sun enter
into the house of the emperor?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A staged counter-question that prepares the answer to step 27.
steps.kashyaTarget: The emperor's assumption that one thing cannot be in many places.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By pretending the servant could block the sun, he gets the emperor to admit the sun is everywhere.

steps.title: The emperor: the sun shines on the whole world
steps.stepSummary: קיסר answers that the sun rests on the entire world; nobody can stop it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: The sun rests upon the whole world.
steps.whatsHappening: The emperor answers the question about the sun, and without realizing it, gives away the answer to his own challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By admitting that the one sun is in every place at once, the emperor has accepted the exact idea he was mocking. רבן גמליאל will now use it.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: שִׁמְשָׁא אַכּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא נָיְחָא.
phrases.english: He said to him: The sun rests upon the whole world.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: שִׁמְשָׁא אַכּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא נָיְחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the sun in step 28.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The sun shines on the entire world at once and cannot be kept out.

steps.title: If one of God's servants fills the world, surely His שכינה does
steps.stepSummary: רבן גמליאל makes a קל וחומר: the sun is just one of countless servants before God and still rests everywhere, so God's שכינה certainly can.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the sun, just one of thousands upon thousands of myriads of servants before הקדוש ברוך הוא, rests upon the whole world, the שכינה of הקדוש ברוך הוא all the more so.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן גמליאל finishes his argument and answers the emperor's mocking question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a קל וחומר: if a small created thing like the sun can be everywhere at once, the Creator surely can. So the שכינה resting on every minyan does not mean there are many שכינות.

keyTerms.meaning: And if (opening of a קל וחומר)

steps.whatToRemember: One thing can be present everywhere at once. Even the sun does it, so God's שכינה certainly can be with every group of ten.

phrases.aramaic: וּמָה שִׁמְשָׁא דְּחַד מִן אֶלֶף אַלְפֵי רִבּוֹא שַׁמָּשֵׁי
phrases.english: And if the sun, which is one of thousands of thousands of myriads of servants
that stand before the Holy One, Blessed be He,
rests upon the whole world,
the Divine Presence of the Holy One, Blessed be He,
all the more so.
phrases.notes: The words left unsaid: all the more so it rests on the whole world.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמָה שִׁמְשָׁא דְּחַד מִן אֶלֶף אַלְפֵי רִבּוֹא שַׁמָּשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the emperor's admission in step 29 to answer his challenge in step 27.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The שכינה can rest on every group of ten without there being more than one; if the sun can fill the world, God's Presence certainly can.

steps.title: A heretic calls God a jester over Ezekiel's commands
steps.stepSummary: A heretic tells רבי אבהו that God is a jester, since He told יחזקאל to lie on his left side and then on his right side.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain heretic said to רבי אבהו: Your God is a jester, since He told יחזקאל 'Lie on your left side,' and it is written 'Lie on your right side'!
steps.whatsHappening: A new story begins. A heretic mocks God, saying the commands to יחזקאל look like a joke.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The heretic points to two commands where God has the נביא lie on one side and then switch to the other. To him, this looks pointless and funny, as if God were playing games.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָהוּא מִינָא לְרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ:
phrases.english: A certain heretic said to Rabbi Abbahu:
Your God is a jester,
as He said to Ezekiel:
"Lie on your left side,"
phrases.notes: יחזקאל 4:4

phrases.english: and it is written: "Lie on your right side"!
phrases.notes: יחזקאל 4:6

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָהוּא מִינָא לְרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: אֱלֹהֵיכֶם גַּחֲכָן הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story with a new challenge from a heretic.
steps.kashyaTarget: God's commands to יחזקאל in יחזקאל chapter 4.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Making the נביא switch from one side to the other seems meaningless, as if God were joking.

steps.title: A student asks the reason for שמיטה
steps.stepSummary: While the heretic is there, a student comes to רבי אבהו and asks why there is a מצוה of שמיטה.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain student came and said to him: What is the reason for the Seventh Year?
steps.whatsHappening: A second person walks in with a different question, about the reason for שמיטה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At first this seems unrelated to the heretic's complaint. The גמרא puts the two questions side by side because רבי אבהו is about to answer both with one explanation.

phrases.english: A certain student came,
and said to him: What is the reason for the Seventh Year?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second question arrives alongside the heretic's challenge in step 31.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason behind the מצוה of שמיטה.

steps.title: רבי אבהו prepares one answer for both questions
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו says he will now tell them something that fits both the heretic and the student.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Now I will tell you something that works for both of you.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. רבי אבהו announces that one explanation will answer both questions, and the actual answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing is answered yet. The point here is that the heretic's complaint about יחזקאל and the student's question about שמיטה are connected, and the next part will show how.

phrases.english: He said to them: Now I will tell you
something that is fit for the two of you.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't look for the answer in this line. רבי אבהו only promises it here; the explanation linking יחזקאל and שמיטה comes in steps 34 and 35.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets up a single answer to both step 31 and step 32.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One explanation will answer both the heretic's complaint and the student's question.

steps.title: Why there is שמיטה: the land belongs to God
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו answers the student. God commanded six years of planting and a seventh year of rest so ישראל would know the land is His. They did not keep it, so they sinned and were exiled.
steps.simpleTranslation: God told ישראל: plant for six years and let the land rest in the seventh, so you will know the land is Mine. But they did not do this. They sinned and were sent into exile.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו starts his promised answer by explaining to the student why the מצוה of שמיטה exists.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason for שמיטה is to show that the land really belongs to God, not to the farmer. This also sets up the second half of the answer: ישראל did not keep שמיטה, which leads to exile and to יחזקאל's suffering.

keyTerms.meaning: And let the land rest (keep שמיטה)

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Israel:
Plant for six years and let the land rest in the seventh,
so that you will know that the land is Mine.
But they did not do so;
rather, they sinned and were exiled.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Carries out the answer רבי אבהו promised in step 33, beginning with the student's question.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why is there a מצוה of שמיטה?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: So that ישראל will know the land belongs to God; failing to keep it led to sin and exile.

steps.title: The merciful king: יחזקאל suffers to cleanse ישראל
steps.stepSummary: A human king whose province rebels kills everyone if cruel, half if merciful, and only makes the leaders suffer if very merciful. In the same way, God made יחזקאל suffer to wipe away ישראל's sins.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is how the world works: when a province rebels against a human king, a cruel king kills them all. A merciful king kills half. A very merciful king only makes the leaders suffer. In the same way, God made יחזקאל suffer to clean away the sins of ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו now answers the heretic: God was not joking with יחזקאל; his lying on his sides was a punishment that spared the people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The heretic said God was a jester for telling יחזקאל to lie on one side and then the other. רבי אבהו shows it was serious: the leader suffers instead of the whole nation. This shows God's great mercy, not mockery.
steps.whatToRemember: One answer for both: שמיטה shows the land is God's, and יחזקאל's suffering was God's mercy, cleansing ישראל's sin of not keeping שמיטה.

phrases.english: The way of the world is:

phrases.aramaic: מֶלֶךְ בָּשָׂר וָדָם שֶׁסָּרְחָה עָלָיו מְדִינָה –
phrases.english: a flesh-and-blood king whose province rebelled against him –

phrases.aramaic: אִם אַכְזָרִי הוּא, הוֹרֵג אֶת כּוּלָּן;
phrases.english: if he is cruel, he kills all of them;
if he is merciful, he kills half of them;
if he is merciful and full of mercy,
he makes the leaders among them suffer with pain.

phrases.aramaic: אַף כָּךְ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְיַיסֵּר אֶת יְחֶזְקֵאל
phrases.english: So too, the Holy One, Blessed be He, makes יחזקאל suffer
in order to wipe away the sins of Israel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the exile from step 34 to answer the heretic's challenge from step 31.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining the purpose behind the seemingly strange command (a משל of a merciful king).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The heretic thought God's command to יחזקאל was a meaningless joke.
steps.terutzMaskana: It was suffering placed on the leader to atone for the whole nation, an act of great mercy.

steps.title: A heretic mocks: where did God immerse after burying משה?
steps.stepSummary: A heretic says God is a כהן because the פסוק says 'take for Me תרומה.' A כהן who touches a dead body must immerse, so after burying משה, where did God immerse? Not in water, since all water fits in His palm.
steps.simpleTranslation: A heretic said to רבי אבהו: Your God is a כהן, since it says 'take for Me תרומה.' When He buried משה, where did He immerse? If you say in water, it says 'Who measured the waters in the hollow of His hand' — all the water is too small for Him.
steps.whatsHappening: A new heretic comes with a mocking challenge, trying to make God look like a limited כהן who has no way to become pure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He builds a trap from two פסוקים. One makes God a כהן who takes תרומה and so must be pure after burying משה; the other shows that all the water in the world is only a handful for God, so He can't immerse in it.

keyTerms.meaning: In the hollow of His hand

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָהוּא מִינָא לְרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ:
phrases.english: A certain heretic said to רבי אבהו:
Your God is a priest,
as it is written: 'That they take for Me תרומה.'
phrases.notes: שמות 25:2. תרומה is normally given to a כהן, so he jokes that God must be one.

phrases.english: When He buried משה, in what did He immerse?
phrases.notes: A כהן who becomes impure from a dead body must immerse before eating תרומה.

phrases.english: And if you say in water,
but isn't it written: 'Who measured the waters in the hollow of His hand'?
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 40:12. All the world's water fits in His palm, so there isn't enough to immerse in.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָהוּא מִינָא לְרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new heretic-and-חכם exchange with רבי אבהו.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If God is a כהן who became impure, He needs a מקוה, yet no water is big enough for Him.

steps.title: God immerses in fire
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו answers that God immersed in fire, as the פסוק says God comes in fire.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said to him: He immersed in fire, as it says: 'For behold, God will come in fire.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו turns the joke around: God doesn't need water, He immerses in fire.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of arguing with the heretic's setup, רבי אבהו answers inside his own game, using a פסוק that connects God with fire. This avoids the problem that water is too small for Him.

phrases.english: He said to him: He immersed in fire,
as it is written: 'For behold, God will come in fire.'
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 66:15

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the heretic's challenge in step 36.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternate means: fire instead of water.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Immersion must be in water, and no water is enough for God.

steps.title: Does immersing in fire even work?
steps.stepSummary: The heretic pushes back: is immersion in fire valid at all?
steps.simpleTranslation: Does immersion in fire really work?
steps.whatsHappening: The heretic challenges רבי אבהו's answer, since normally purifying is done in water.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The attack is now on the method itself. In הלכה we know of immersing in a מקוה of water, so fire seems like it doesn't count.

phrases.english: But does immersion in fire work?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 37.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אבהו's claim that God immersed in fire.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Purifying is normally done in water, so fire seems invalid.

steps.title: Fire is the main way of purifying
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו answers that fire is actually the main purifier, since the פסוק says that only what cannot go through fire should go through water.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Just the opposite! The main purifying is in fire, as it says: 'And whatever cannot go into the fire, pass it through water.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו defends his answer and even makes it stronger, proving fire is the first choice for purifying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about cleaning the vessels taken from מדין puts fire first, and water is only for things that can't handle fire. So fire is the stronger way to purify, not a weaker one.

keyTerms.meaning: On the contrary / just the opposite

steps.whatToRemember: רבי אבהו answers the mocking heretic from his own פסוקים: God 'immerses' in fire, and fire is the main purifier.

phrases.english: He said to him: On the contrary,
the main immersion is in fire,
as it is written: 'And whatever cannot come into the fire,
phrases.notes: במדבר 31:23

phrases.english: you shall pass through the water.'
phrases.notes: Fire comes first; water is only for things that can't go into fire.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַדְּרַבָּה, עִיקַּר טְבִילוּתָא בְּנוּרָא הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 38 and closes this exchange.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reversal (אדרבה): the challenged method is actually the main one.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Fire does not count as purifying; only water does.
steps.terutzMaskana: Fire is the primary way of purifying, water is secondary.

steps.title: A heretic asks what makes ישראל special
steps.stepSummary: A heretic tells רבי אבינא: the פסוק calls ישראל a unique nation, but what is your greatness? You are counted together with us, since 'all the nations are like nothing before Him.'
steps.simpleTranslation: A heretic said to רבי אבינא: It says 'Who is like Your people ישראל, one nation in the land.' What is so great about you? You are also mixed in with us, as it says: 'All the nations are like nothing before Him.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new heretic challenges a different חכם, claiming one פסוק cancels out the specialness of ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He reads 'all the nations' as including ישראל. If every nation is nothing before God, then ישראל is no greater than anyone else, which seems to contradict the פסוק praising ישראל.

keyTerms.meaning: You are mixed in with us

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָהוּא מִינָא לְרַבִּי אֲבִינָא:
phrases.english: A certain heretic said to רבי אבינא:

phrases.aramaic: כְּתִיב ״וּמִי כְעַמְּךָ כְּיִשְׂרָאֵל גּוֹי אֶחָד בָּאָרֶץ״,
phrases.english: It is written: 'And who is like Your people, Israel, one nation in the land,'
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 7:23

phrases.english: What is your greatness?
phrases.notes: Literally 'their greatness'; he means the greatness of you Jews.

phrases.english: You too are mixed in with us,
as it is written: 'All the nations are like nothing before Him.'
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 40:17

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָהוּא מִינָא לְרַבִּי אֲבִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new exchange, now with רבי אבינא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The uniqueness of ישראל stated in שמואל ב 7:23.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'All the nations' includes ישראל, so ישראל is nothing special.

steps.title: רבי אבינא: one of your own testified for us
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבינא begins his answer: someone from your own side already testified about us, as a פסוק says. The quote continues on the next part of the daf.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: One of your own people already testified about us, as it is written…
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבינא starts answering, and the גמרא is setting up a פסוק that will be quoted next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rather than arguing alone, רבי אבינא points to a witness from the non-Jewish side who praised ישראל. The actual פסוק comes right after this line.

phrases.english: He said to him: One of your own has testified about us,
as it is written:
phrases.notes: The פסוק itself comes at the start of the next section of the daf.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the heretic's challenge from step 40.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Proof from the challenger's own side.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ישראל is no greater than the other nations.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even a non-Jewish witness praised ישראל (the פסוק follows next).
